Hardware devices are grouped by what they do. Input devices get data into a computer: a microphone captures sound, a mouse controls the pointer, a graphics digitiser captures freehand drawing with a stylus, and a touch screen lets users select options by touching the display. Output devices present information: speakers produce sound, a laser printer produces high-quality pages, and a 3D printer builds solid objects. Storage devices keep data permanently, even when the power is off: hard disc drives store data magnetically, solid state drives use flash memory, and high-definition optical discs such as Blu-ray use a laser. A touch screen is unusual because it is both an input and an output device.
Makes sense. Keep going.

No device is best in every situation. A device is chosen by matching its features to the task, the users and the environment. A microphone is ideal for a gamer chatting to teammates, but voice input would be a poor choice in a noisy school canteen. Exam questions nearly always give a scenario, so every advantage you give should be linked to it.
Right. What else do we need to know?

A microphone turns sound into an electrical signal that is converted into digital data. It is used for voice recognition, such as dictating text or giving commands to a smart speaker, as well as for video calls, recording music and online gaming headsets. Speaking is faster than typing and is hands-free, but background noise reduces accuracy and sound files need much more storage than text. A mouse uses sensors to detect movement and moves the on-screen pointer. It is easy to learn, but needs a flat surface, and experienced users often find keyboard shortcuts quicker. A graphics digitiser is a flat pad used with a stylus, much like a pencil on paper.
Got it. Keep going.

It gives more natural and more accurate drawing than a mouse, which suits artists and designers, and it can also capture signatures. However, it is more expensive than a mouse and poor for selecting menus. A touch screen has a touch-sensitive glass surface. A touch changes the electrical signal, and the position is worked out as x, y co-ordinates. Touch screens need little skill and are quick, but they get dirty and can only show a limited number of options.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

Speakers turn electrical signals from the sound card into sound. They are used for music, video, games and alert sounds, and they help visually impaired users by reading text aloud. Their main drawback is that they can disturb others nearby, so headphones may be better in shared spaces. A laser printer receives the page as data. A laser beam draws the page onto a drum as a pattern of static charge, powdered toner sticks to the charged areas, and the toner is transferred to paper and fixed with heat.
Okay. Keep going.

Laser printers are fast for large volumes and give sharp text and graphics, which is why schools and offices use them. However, colour models are expensive to buy and run, and because they are non-impact printers they cannot print multipart carbon-copy forms. A 3D printer builds a solid object one layer at a time from a CAD design, using materials such as plastic, metal or ceramics. It is ideal for prototypes and custom items such as prosthetic hands, but it is slow for large objects and not yet economical for mass production.
Go on.

A hard disc drive (HDD) contains rigid magnetic discs, called platters, sealed in a case to keep dust out. Each surface is split into circular tracks and the tracks into sectors, and read/write heads move across the spinning discs to reach data. HDDs offer very large capacities at the lowest cost per gigabyte, but their moving parts can fail or be damaged if dropped, and access is slower than flash storage. A solid state drive (SSD) uses flash memory with no moving parts. It is non-volatile, much faster, quiet, light, uses less power and survives knocks, but costs more per gigabyte.
Right. Keep going.

Other flash storage includes USB drives, memory cards for phones and cameras, and the smart-card chips in bank cards and door entry cards. High-definition storage media, such as Blu-ray, are optical discs. A blue-violet laser has a shorter wavelength than the red laser in a DVD drive, so the pits are smaller and packed more tightly, and a dual-layer disc holds 50 gigabytes. They suit HD films and games, but scratch easily.

Output device?

Marks are given for a valid point that is clearly explained and linked to the scenario. 'An SSD is faster' may get one mark; 'an SSD has no moving parts, so the inspector's laptop is less likely to be damaged if dropped' gets more. Make your points comparative, such as 'lower cost per gigabyte than an SSD'. Do not give the same idea twice in different words, and avoid vague answers such as 'it is better' or 'it is easier'. Learn the key facts: 3D printers work layer by layer, laser printers use toner, HDDs are magnetic and SSDs have no moving parts.
